item.title: Preserving Orientation and Transition Order in Transition Network Analysis: A Directed Topological Proof of Concept
item.description: arXiv:2611.28249v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transition Network Analysis (TNA; tna, Nestimate) models learning as directed Markov transitions. While Nestimate also offers sequence-level higher-order models, clique-based topological tools lose directional structure: tna::cliques() returns unordered mutual subsets without homology or convergence-divergence asymmetry, and undirected persistent homology in Nestimate symmetrizes transitions into clique complexes, erasing edge orientation and triangle order. We evaluate four directed constructions on group_regulation (9 states): Dowker sink/source complexes, directed flag complexes ($dFl$), and regular GLMY path homology, compared against row-permutation and degree-preserving null models ($B = 20,000$). Across $\tau \in [0.20, 0.28]$, $\beta_1^{dFl}$ exceeds the max-symmetrized clique complex $\beta_1^{\mathrm{sym}}$ by $1$; on $\tau \in (0.239087, 0.290401]$ (e.g., $\tau = 0.26$), $\beta_1^{\mathrm{sym}} = 0$ whereas $\beta_1^{dFl} = 1$, capturing the reciprocal consensus $\leftrightarrow$ plan loop (weights $0.3958, 0.2904$). On $\tau \in (0.146825, 0.172081]$, $dFl$ also leaves the directed 3-cycle {consensus, coregulate, emotion} unfilled. Regular GLMY path homology gives $\beta_1^{\mathrm{path}} = 0$ across all thresholds (lower-tail $p = 0.012$ for its sum over $[0.14, 0.30]$ under row permutation, reflecting in-degree concentration). Dowker analysis reveals significant sink-source asymmetry: 20-21 sink vs. 0 source 2-simplices across $[0.20, 0.28]$ ($p = 0.002$ at $\tau = 0.26$), driven by six behaviors converging onto consensus ($\mathrm{InStrength} = 2.667$). Thus, directed complexes unify feedback and sink convergence over one directed graph.
item.dc:creator: Koichi Yasutake, Hitoshi Inoue

item.title: Beyond Invoice Volumes: Temporal Network Structure, Maturity Concentration, and Systemic Liquidity Exposure in SME Trade-Credit Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.28876v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Trade-credit invoices encode directed obligations whose temporal synchronization and counterparty concentration are obscured by annual volume totals. We audit 749,952 atomic B2B invoices from 2012-2023 (EUR 99.705B; 75,343 firms) from the pseudonymized Mendeley Data corpus (Esteva de la Rosa, 2026), separating 1,240 terminal 2024 bridge records (EUR 630.12M; 9 bridge-only firms) and 13 extreme-duration contracts (>3,650 days; EUR 297.75k). Using directed weighted graphs, HHI, Shannon entropy, CR1 shares, spectral centralities, and multi-cadence temporal operators, we formulate and benchmark a Maturity-Aware Network Exposure (MANE) indicator. Invoice values are heavily skewed: the top 1% hold 81.41% of value (Gini = 0.9742). Two-way fixed-effects panels with circular block bootstrapping ($B=999$, 12-month blocks) and Holm-Bonferroni control show higher lagged debtor counterparty concentration is associated with lower MANE ($\hat{\beta}=-0.494$, 95% CI $[-0.752,-0.248]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.004$). Robustness audits (R1-R4) confirm stability under 2021 exclusion ($-0.402$, $p=0.004$), Shannon entropy ($+0.257$), CR1 ($-0.515$), 1%-99% Winsorization ($-0.462$, all $p=0.001$), and multi-invoice debtors (count $\ge 2$, $-0.334$, $p=0.031$). Conversely, within-FE diagnostics expose severe joint-concentration multicollinearity (VIF = 22.22) that vanishes for multi-invoice debtors ($p=0.719$), while regime splits reveal a macro reciprocity sign reversal between 2012-2019 ($-0.706$) and 2020-2023 ($+0.232$, both $p=0.001$). In 12-month purged forecasting, MANE does not reliably improve over maturity seeds ($\Delta\mathrm{MSE}=2.668$, 95% CI $[-0.027,7.954]$; trimmed $0.067$, $[-0.035,0.194]$), positioning MANE as a reproducible screening and auditing diagnostic, rather than a default proxy, for supply-chain finance, multilateral clearing, and RWA tokenization.
item.dc:creator: Sai Srikanth Madugula, Peplluis Esteva de la Rosa, Daya Shankar

item.title: Religious expression and well-being across countries and regions: Evidence from a decade of social media posts
item.description: arXiv:2611.28908v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study examines whether social connectedness constitutes a pathway between religious expression and subsequent well-being. Drawing on millions of social-media posts, we combine broad international coverage, subnational geographic detail, and annual observations over 2013-2022 to examine religious expression, connectedness, and three well-being dimensions. The longitudinal models account for baseline connectedness and well-being, geographic and year effects, and national trends. National longitudinal models support positive indirect associations through social connectedness for happiness and life satisfaction. The indirect estimates for purpose nationally and for all three outcomes regionally are positive but imprecise. Complementary coefficient contrasts in contemporaneous regional models and comparisons of regional period averages show stronger associations of religious expression with purpose than with either happiness or life satisfaction. Together, these findings support a national pathway through social connectedness for the affective and evaluative dimensions of well-being. The stronger regional associations with purpose motivate further investigation of meaning- and direction-related processes beyond the measured connectedness pathway.
item.dc:creator: Stefano Maria Iacus, Giuseppe Porro, Haodong Qi

item.title: Community Detection in Fuzzy Social Networks through Fuzzy Co-Membership Relations over Alpha-Cut Realizations
item.description: arXiv:2611.29342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In fuzzy social networks the ties between actors are triangular fuzzy numbers, and community detection applied to their cores ignores how the partition depends on their vagueness. We propose a fuzzy co-membership relation obtained by running the Louvain algorithm on crisp networks compatible with the alpha-cuts of the ties and integrating the proportions of co-assignment over alpha. The relation is positive semidefinite; from it we derive a consensus partition, the number of groups, membership degrees and an assignment ambiguity index. In simulations from stochastic block models the relation does not yield better partitions than symmetric perturbations of the cores of the same size. Its ambiguity index is more closely associated with the structural position of the actors and identifies actors split between two groups when the vagueness is concentrated on them; when the asymmetry of the fuzzy ties points towards the latent tie strength, its co-membership degrees have a lower Brier score. The interval-weighted Louvain algorithm estimates the number of communities more accurately. In two departmental collaboration networks the observed ambiguity is lower than under permuted ratings, while the partitions depend on the symmetrization of directed ratings and on the coding of non-response.
item.dc:creator: Annamaria Porreca, Fabrizio Maturo

item.title: BiLight: A Fast Method for Estimating Counts of 6-Vertex Bipartite Motifs in Large Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.30249v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motifs, or small subgraphs, are fundamental building blocks of complex networks. Analyzing their frequency distribution provides deep insights into the local structure of graphs, with applications in social network analysis, bioinformatics, and web mining. However, exact enumeration of motifs becomes computationally expensive as the size of the motif and the network increases. This challenge is particularly acute for bipartite motifs, which are ubiquitous in modeling relationships like user-item, author-paper, and actor-movie interactions. In this work, we present BiLight (Bipartite Lightweight motif estimation), a scalable framework for estimating the frequencies of all 17 non-isomorphic 6-vertex bipartite motifs. Specifically, we focus on estimating the non-induced counts of these motifs, which is a common requirement in many graph mining tasks. Our approach relies on a randomized path sampling of paths on four vertices. We use an efficient, weighted strategy by counting the ways that each sampled path can be extended to one of the 17 motifs. This framework yields unbiased estimates of the global motif counts. We conduct extensive experiments on networks of various sizes. Our experiments demonstrate that BiLight converges rapidly to the ground truth with high accuracy, even on massive networks where exact counting is infeasible. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/celikmustaa/BiLight.
item.dc:creator: Mustafa \c{C}elik, \"Ozg\"ur Okumu\c{s}, Lale \"Ozkahya

item.title: The Humming Revachol: A Dialogue Network Analysis of Narrative Power in Disco Elysium
item.description: arXiv:2611.28812v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This study applies social network analysis to the narrative RPG Disco Elysium to examine how narrative power is distributed among its characters. A directed, weighted character-mention network of 73 NPCs is constructed from the game's complete dialogue script, with characters identified and annotated across five social attributes. Narrative power is operationalised through four dimensions: attention, authority, discursive initiative, and embeddedness. Non-parametric statistical tests examine differences across gender, age, race, class, and ideology. The findings suggest that narrative power is largely independent of social identity categories and is more closely associated with character narrative functions, while structural embeddedness reflects the socio-organisational contexts in which characters are situated. These findings show that dialogue-network analysis can reveal structural patterns of representation that visibility counts alone would miss.
item.dc:creator: Xinran Liu, Miguel Arana-Catania, Jack Orchard

item.title: S\'anchez, Feij\'oo, or Abascal? Speaker Attribution and Ideological Congruence in LLM Personas Reading Posts on X of the Leaders of the Three Main Parties of the 29N General Election in Spain
item.description: arXiv:2611.29765v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Source cues are central to political communication, yet reception studies with large language model (LLM) personas as synthetic audiences have not tested whether personas respond to who speaks and not only to what is said. With Spain's general election of 29 November 2026 in mind, we run a speaker-attribution experiment using 1,075 anonymised X posts by the leaders of PSOE, PP and VOX on four topics (the economy and employment, household costs, immigration and corruption) and 791 distinct value-grounded, LLM-generated personas. Each post was assigned to 300 topic-selected persona profiles, 150 grounded in the Inglehart-Welzel cultural map and 150 in Moral Foundations Theory, under four conditions: no author, S\'anchez, Feij\'oo or Abascal, yielding 322,470 complete persona-post quartets. Naming any leader lowered support for identical text, with the penalty for Abascal nearly twice as large as those for S\'anchez and Feij\'oo. The penalty follows the persona's elicited left-right self-placement (ideological congruence): left personas spare S\'anchez and right personas spare Feij\'oo, although ideology was never in the message-evaluation prompt. Corruption posts were penalised under every name, whereas on other topics the ideologically closest leader generally produced little or no penalty. The leader order matches public opinion in 48 CIS barometers (2022-2026) in all three groups and the sign of all twelve differences, but fits barometers before the model's 2024 knowledge cutoff better than recent ones. Our findings demonstrate that LLM personas evaluate political speakers through systematic, value-congruent priors: however, while they replicate human candidate rank-orders across survey barometers, this alignment is ordinal rather than quantitative, highlighting their utility for controlled source-effect experiments though not as substitutes for empirical public opinion surveys.
item.dc:creator: V\'ictor Yeste, Candida Maria Greco, Paolo Rosso, Andrea Tagarelli

item.title: Matching Under Metric Privacy
item.description: arXiv:2611.31208v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study how to represent and randomize points in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space to obtain accurate bipartite matchings under metric privacy. Given $n$ private and $n$ public points, we analyze local mechanisms that randomize each private point or its distances to the public points. Using the public points' affine span, we construct a smaller representation that preserves all matching costs. When a trusted server receives the private points, we establish privacy and utility guarantees for Gumbel matching, which randomizes edge costs and releases only the assignment. Through upper bounds and worst-case constructions, we establish the tight rate $\Theta\!\left(n\min\{d,\log n\}/\varepsilon\right)$ for expected cost above the nonprivate optimum. Benchmark experiments support $d\approx\log n$ as a practical guide to the transition between directly randomizing point coordinates and using Gumbel matching. Extensions to squared Euclidean costs enable private nonparametric two-sample hypothesis testing. These results show how the application's trust model guides representation and dimension choices for better utility: under local privacy, low-dimensional point representations reduce excess cost, while under central privacy, distance representations achieve the optimal rate even in high dimension.
item.dc:creator: Hongyi B. Hu, Dung Nguyen, M. Amin Rahimian

item.title: LLM-Enhanced Rumor Detection via Virtual Node Induced Edge Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2602.13279v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The rapid proliferation of rumors on social networks poses a significant threat to information integrity. While rumor dissemination forms complex structural patterns, existing detection methods often fail to capture the intricate interplay between textual coherence and propagation dynamics. Current approaches typically represent nodes through isolated textual embeddings, neglecting the semantic flow across the entire propagation path. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel framework that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) as a structural augmentation layer for graph-based rumor detection. Moving beyond conventional methods, our framework employs LLMs to evaluate information subchains and strategically introduce a virtual node into the graph. This structural modification converts latent semantic patterns into explicit topological features, effectively capturing the textual coherence that has historically been inaccessible to Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). To ensure reliability, we develop a structured prompt framework that mitigates inherent biases in LLMs while maintaining robust graph learning performance. Furthermore, our proposed framework is model-agnostic, meaning it is not constrained to any specific graph learning algorithm or LLMs. Its plug-and-play nature allows for seamless integration with further fine-tuned LLMs and graph techniques in the future, potentially enhancing predictive performance without the need to modify original algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Jiran Tao, Cheng Wang, Binyan Jiang

item.title: Structural Hallucination in Large Language Models: A Network-Based Evaluation of Knowledge Organization and Citation Integrity
item.description: arXiv:2603.01341v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly mediate access to scholarly information, yet their outputs are typically evaluated at the level of individual statements rather than knowledge structure. This paper introduces structural hallucination: distortion of conceptual organization, relational architecture, and bibliographic grounding that remains invisible to sentence-level accuracy metrics. We develop a network-based stress test grounded in knowledge graph extraction, graph similarity analysis, centrality comparison, and citation integrity verification. The protocol is applied to three structured domains representing core forms of scholarly knowledge: Roget's Thesaurus (1911) as a historical knowledge organization system; Wikidata philosophers as a biographical knowledge graph; and bibliographic citation records from Dimensions.ai. Across all domains, substantial structural divergence is observed. In the lexical benchmark, pooled F1 scores range from 0.07 to 0.15; in the biographical benchmark, 40-90% of generated values are absent from Wikidata and DBpedia; and in the bibliometric benchmark, citation omission reaches 100%. Network-level comparison in the Roget reconstruction reveals node-set Jaccard similarity of 0.088 and a source-mismatch rate of 71%. These findings show that structural fidelity cannot be inferred from local fluency. The proposed stress test provides a reproducible instrument for evaluating the structural integrity of LLM-generated knowledge representations within knowledge organization and information quality research.
item.dc:creator: Moses Boudourides

item.title: LLMs for Qualitative and Mixed-Methods Social Network Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2607.14045v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This manuscript explores the integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into the field of qualitative and mixed-methods social network analysis (SNA). We argue that the primary focus of this integration should be on enhancing the depth and rigor of qualitative SNA, rather than on replacing human researchers with automated systems. We begin by outlining the core principles of qualitative and mixed-methods SNA, emphasizing the importance of understanding the meaning of ties, the role of narratives, and the significance of relational identities. We then discuss how LLMs can be used as powerful tools to augment this work, from assisting with data collection and coding to supporting theory-building and abductive reasoning. We also address the limitations and ethical challenges of using LLMs in this context, including issues of bias, hallucination, and the need for reflexivity. We conclude with a series of research designs and practical recommendations for researchers who want to integrate LLMs into their work in a thoughtful and responsible way.
item.dc:creator: Moses Boudourides

item.title: Growing Hypergraphs with Homophily
item.description: arXiv:2607.16046v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: There are many extant models of hypergraphs with interactions governed by attribute-based homophily between nodes, but most assume independence between edges conditional on node parameters. Relaxing this assumption, we study a mechanistic model of growing hypergraphs in which edge formation is influenced by both previous edges and binary node labels. Edges form in this model as noisy copies of previous edges, where the transmission of nodes from one edge to the next depends on multiple homophilic mechanisms between labels. These homophilic mechanisms give rise to tunable assortative structure in the hypergraph. We derive a power law for the degree distribution in this model and describe the long-term dynamics of the joint distribution of labels contained in edges. Our model defines a likelihood over a labeled hypergraph, allowing us to use standard maximum-likelihood techniques to structure algorithms. We estimate the model parameters on synthetic and real data via (stochastic) expectation maximization. These estimates give statistically-principled descriptions of the operation of homophily in empirical polyadic systems. We also demonstrate an approach to community detection via simulated annealing which, though computationally expensive, achieves competitive results on both synthetic data and certain empirical data sets known to be challenging to community detection techniques based on the edge-independence assumption. Our findings highlight the benefits of incorporating edge- and label-dependence in higher-order modeling and data analysis, and point to several directions for future work.
item.dc:creator: Violet Ross, Francis Cataldo, Philip S. Chodrow

item.title: Investigating Forecasting Capabilities of Narrative Networks on Emerging Stories
item.description: arXiv:2610.35628v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Networks have been used to model the interactions among the elements that underlie a narrative. In this paper, we investigate whether the structure of these networks can predict which links will emerge as a storyline evolves. We construct these networks from news articles using a Semantic Edge Parser (SEP) built on a Large Language Model (LLM), and evaluate the networks on three disparate real-world storylines, the 2022 Canadian Freedom Convoy, Hurricane Melissa (2025), and the 2025-26 Iranian protests. To test the narrative network's predictive capability, we construct a rolling window of the narrative and predict the emergent links between existing narrative elements on the day following the rolling window period. We identify candidate links with seven standard link predictors, including the Adamic-Adar index, Common Neighbors, and Preferential Attachment. Forecasting next-day links across the three storylines, we find Preferential Attachment to be the strongest standard link predictor, achieving a mean ROC-AUC of 0.76-0.79. It exceeds EdgeBank, a memorization baseline, by 11.3-14.5 points on every event. To summarize, narrative-network structure ranks next-day emergent relations above chance, though this advantage is concentrated among the most frequently mentioned, highly connected entities.
item.dc:creator: Ravi Teja Karumuri, Steven Corman, Huan Liu, Joshua Garland

item.title: Learn to Vaccinate: Combining Structure Learning and Effective Vaccination for Epidemic and Outbreak Control
item.description: arXiv:2506.15397v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) model is a widely used model for the spread of information and infectious diseases, particularly non-immunizing ones, on a graph. Given a highly contagious disease, a natural question is how to best vaccinate individuals to minimize the disease's extinction time. While previous works showed that the problem of optimal vaccination is closely linked to the NP-hard Spectral Radius Minimization (SRM) problem, they assumed that the graph is known, which is often not the case in practice. In this work, we consider the problem of minimizing the extinction time of an outbreak modeled by an SIS model where the graph on which the disease spreads is unknown and only the infection states of the vertices are observed. To this end, we split the problem into two: learning the graph and determining effective vaccination strategies. We propose a novel inclusion-exclusion-based learning algorithm and, unlike previous approaches, establish its sample complexity for graph recovery. We then detail an optimal SRM algorithm whose running time is polynomial in the number of vertices for bounded treewidth and a fixed vaccination budget. This is complemented by an efficient and effective polynomial-time greedy heuristic for any graph. Finally, we present experiments on synthetic and real-world data that numerically validate our learning and vaccination algorithms.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025), PMLR 267
item.dc:creator: Sepehr Elahi, Paula M\"urmann, Patrick Thiran

item.title: Temporal connection probabilities in real networks
item.description: arXiv:2604.23714v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Principled prediction of when and where links form in complex networks is a fundamental problem. We derive a closed-form non-Markovian expression for next-step connection probabilities that unifies latent hyperbolic geometry with long-range memory of past interactions. This expression yields interpretable forecasts governed by a small set of parameters. Applied to large-scale real networks, the framework explains how interaction history changes the distance dependence of connectivity: repeated interactions can remain probable at large distances, whereas first-contact probabilities are consistent with a nonmonotonic distance dependence. The framework's predictions agree quantitatively with empirical connection probabilities. These results provide a common probabilistic description of first contacts and repeated interactions, linking the latent geometry of networks to their temporal connectivity.
item.dc:creator: Fragkiskos Papadopoulos

item.title: Hierarchical Possession-Aware Graph Pointer Network for Pass Receiver Selection
item.description: arXiv:2609.04803v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Pass receiver selection is a fundamental task in football analytics, aiming to predict the intended receiver under a given game state. This task is challenging with event-centered freeze-frame observations, a broadcast-like setting that provides only partial and variable player visibility without complete trajectories or stable player identities. The model must therefore reason over anonymous visible candidates, opponent pressure, and recent context under partial observation. To address this setting, we propose a Hierarchical Possession-aware Graph Pointer Network (HPGPN), which formulates pass receiver selection as variable-size candidate prediction over visible teammates. HPGPN jointly models current player interactions, local event context, and possession-level temporal dynamics. It represents the current pass situation with a graph, incorporates fixed event context, and uses dynamic possession history to capture how the attacking sequence evolves. Candidate representations are refined hierarchically by integrating spatial, contextual, and historical evidence, and a glimpse pointer head scores the receiver candidates. Experiments on public football event and freeze-frame data show that HPGPN improves pass receiver selection performance. Ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of graph-based interaction modeling, fixed event context, and dual-branch dynamic possession-history modeling.
item.dc:creator: Jingyi Wang, Da Li, Kaixin Wang, Zhangqin Huang

item.title: SeqFold: Timestamp-Addressable Compressed States for User Action Sequence Backbones
item.description: arXiv:2611.13704v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Existing sequential user modeling methods mainly focus on improving the backbone encoder or learning task-specific user representations for a single prediction objective. We instead study how to export the multi-layer user states of a frozen long-history backbone as compact, timestamp-addressable representations for downstream training backfill and serving. In this setting, the user state at a given timestamp summarizes the user's actions before that time, so downstream systems need only the state aligned to each target timestamp rather than the full hidden-state timeline. To this end, we present \texttt{SeqFold}, a compressed-state interface that combines learned multi-channel fusion, channel-specific temporal decay, and Lookup-Free Quantization (LFQ) to produce compact discrete codes from frozen backbone states. Task-specific decoders then map these shared codes into flexible embedding spaces for downstream models. To make timestamp-addressable export practical at scale, we further develop a fused streaming implementation that updates the fusion recurrence after every action while materializing states only at target timestamps. On large-scale proprietary datasets, SeqFold reduces per-state representation storage by $3{,}400\times$ while preserving most of the downstream ranking performance of the uncompressed model, showing that SeqFold is an effective interface for reusing long-history sequence backbones in downstream models.
item.dc:creator: Mianwei Zhou, Duo Zhang, Henry Tsai, Yuqi Zheng, Jian Li, Juexin Lin, Sujay Khandagale, Zheng Zhang, Vijay Rajaram, Dong Jiao, Tao Cheng
